item.title: Xi: National rejuvenation is unstoppable
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
Xi: National rejuvenation is unstoppable President applauds PRC's remarkable achievements at reception in Beijing President Xi Jinping said on Wednesday that the rejuvenation of the Chinese nation is unstoppable and expressed full confidence in the bright prospects for Chinese modernization, on the eve of China's National Day on Oct 1. Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, made the remarks while addressing a reception at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing to celebrate the 77th anniversary of the founding of the People's Republic of China. Xi said that the system of socialism with Chinese characteristics has demonstrated tremendous strengths through long-term exploration and practice, and that China has continued to make progress in modernizing its system and capacity for governance. Reflecting on the past 77 years, Xi said the Party has united and led the Chinese people in tireless efforts, creating the twin miracles of rapid economic development and long-term social stability. China has achieved its first centenary goal of building a moderately prosperous society in all respects and is forging ahead toward its second centenary goal of building a great modern socialist country in all respects, he said. "At this moment, we are immensely proud of the remarkable achievements of New China and fully confident in the bright prospects for Chinese modernization," Xi told around 800 Chinese and foreign guests, including Party and State leaders, foreign envoys, recipients of national honors and dignitaries from all walks of life. Reviewing this year's progress, Xi said the entire Party and the nation have forged ahead with determination and worked tirelessly, formulating and implementing the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), making solid progress across various fields, and effectively responding to risks and challenges. The Chinese economy has continued to advance despite pressures, making progress in innovation-led and high-quality development while demonstrating strong resilience and vitality, he said. New progress and achievements have been made in the cause of the Party and the country, Xi added. Facing complex international and domestic conditions, Xi called for adhering to the general principle of pursuing progress while ensuring stability, fully and faithfully applying the new development philosophy on all fronts, and moving faster to foster a new pattern of development. He urged further deepening reform and opening-up, better coordinating development and security, and promoting continued economic improvement through innovation and higher-quality development. Efforts should also be made to guarantee and improve people's livelihoods, meet the targets and tasks set for the year and ensure a good start to the 15th Five-Year Plan period, he said. Xi stressed the need to unswervingly implement the policy of "one country, two systems", under which the people of Hong Kong administer Hong Kong and the people of Macao administer Macao, both with a high degree of autonomy. He called for supporting Hong Kong and Macao in better integrating into and contributing to the country's overall development, and maintaining their long-term prosperity and stability. On cross-Strait relations, Xi called for deepening exchanges and cooperation, resolutely cracking down on "Taiwan independence" separatist forces and opposing external interference. He also urged efforts to promote the peaceful development of cross-Strait relations and advance the cause of national reunification. On foreign affairs, Xi called for adhering to an independent foreign policy of peace, advancing the implementation of the four global initiatives and promoting the building of a community with a shared future for humanity, in order to inject more certainty and positive energy into a world marked by change and turmoil. "As long as we remain confident, stay focused on our goals and move forward steadily, step by step, success will surely belong to the great Communist Party of China, the great Chinese people and the great People's Republic of China," he said. mojingxi@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Targeting a continental shift
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
Targeting a continental shift China looks to translate Asiad track and field success into results on the global stage On a drizzly morning in Nagoya on Sept 23, a 19-year-old race walker marked a milestone more than five decades in the making. Shi Shengji won the men's half-marathon race walk in one hour, 23 minutes and 32 seconds, finishing four minutes and 29 seconds ahead of Japan's world-record holder Toshikazu Yamanishi. The victory was Shi's first Asian Games gold and China's 200th athletics gold at the continental showpiece. It was a symbolic moment for a team in transition. At the conclusion of the athletics competition on Tuesday, China had collected 17 gold, 14 silver and eight bronze medals thanks to 72 athletes. The haul underlined China's depth across Asian athletics, but the more important question is how much of that success can be carried onto the world stage? With the World Athletics Championships returning to Beijing in 2027, Nagoya offered both encouragement and a reality check. Shi's rise is one of the clearest examples of the new generation of Chinese track and field talent emerging. He switched from middle-distance running to race walking in 2023 and, after three years of focused training, rose rapidly from the youth ranks to the top of the Asian podium. Shi attributed his progress to painstaking technical work. "My coach goes through videos of my technique frame by frame and works on every detail," he said. Yang Liujing, the women's half-marathon race walk champion, has a different narrative, more of a comeback story. After struggling through a difficult period and once considering retirement, the 28-year-old finally secured her first Asian Games gold. Shi's emergence and Yang's resurgence give China both a new prospect and an experienced contender in race walking. But success at the Asian Games does not automatically translate into contention at the world level. The same combination of youth and promise was evident on the running track. Seventeen-year-old Chen Yujie emerged as one of the faces of China's new generation, winning three golds and a silver. She clocked 11.06 seconds to win the women's 100 meters, setting an Asian Games record, before taking silver in the 200m and helping China win both the women's and mixed 4x100m relays. "I always thought the Asian Games success was a dream, but after coming here, I realized it wasn't as unattainable as I had imagined," Chen said. Her confidence has grown quickly, but so have her ambitions. She wants to break 11 seconds before eventually targeting 10.60 to 10.70. "I've gone from being a challenger to a defending champion, and holding on to that title won't be easy," Chen said after winning the 100m. "I want to keep a challenger's mindset and set my sights on the world championships and the Olympics." That will be a far more demanding test. An Asian Games title establishes her as a leading continental sprinter, but breaking into the global elite will require a significant improvement in both speed and consistency. "What I achieved at the Games is a real motivator," Chen said. "Now that it's done, I can already start looking ahead to the next one." China successfully defended its sprint relay titles and also won the mixed 4x100m. Experienced sprinters such as Xie Zhenye and Liang Xiaojing continued to provide stability, while younger runners such as Chen increasingly took on greater responsibility. "Relay is not an individual event. It is the result of the whole team's effort," Xie said. The combination of experience and youth gives China greater depth in an event where teamwork can be as important as individual speed. Chen Yuanjiang also ended China's eight-year wait for the men's 110m hurdles title. His winning time of 13.15 seconds was enough for Asian gold, but the 20-year-old immediately set his sights higher. "It's still not good enough," Chen Yuanjiang said, initially targeting 13.10 before looking to break through the 13-second barrier. His Asian title underlined China's strength in the event, but his own targets point to the gap he still hopes to close. Strength in depth The women's throwing events remain an established strength for China. Chinese athletes swept the gold medals in the women's shot put, discus, javelin and hammer throw, underlining the nation's depth. Eighteen-year-old Yan Ziyi won the javelin with her first and only throw of the final, hitting 70.46 meters and beating Japan's Olympic champion Haruka Kitaguchi. "I'm grateful that people gave me the nickname 'Yan one and done,'" Yan said. "I haven't let them down, and I think I've lived up to it." Her ambition goes beyond Asian titles. "I want China to stand on top (of the world) and start my own era," she said. Her 70-meter-plus form suggests genuine world-medal potential, although consistency against the very best will be the bigger test. Nineteen-year-old Zhang Jiale won the hammer throw, with teammate Zhao Jie taking silver. She twice bettered the Asian record this season, reaching 79.62m. Her next target is 80m, and she hopes to challenge for the title at the world championships in Beijing. At the other end of the age spectrum, 32-year-old Feng Bin defended her discus title with 63.83m. Although the mark fell short of her target in Nagoya, she had thrown a season-best 67.46m to win the Diamond League Final earlier this month. Her aim is to win gold at the home world championships before pursuing Olympic gold in Los Angeles. The results of Yan, Zhang and Feng show why the throwing events remain among China's strongest areas. More importantly, they provide China with a group of athletes with realistic potential to challenge for medals at a global level. The jumping events produced some encouraging signs, too. Su Wen won the men's triple jump with 17.42m, breaking a 36-year-old Asian Games record and reaching the qualifying benchmark for next year's world championships. Shi Yuhao, meanwhile, upgraded his bronze from Hangzhou to gold in the men's long jump, winning with a season-best 8.17m. Neither mark, however, would challenge the world leaders, underlining the gap China still needs to bridge. China's recent world championships record also highlights the challenge of converting Asian success into global glory. At the 2015 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, the team won one gold, seven silvers and one bronze. At the 2025 world championships in Tokyo, it collected just two silvers and two bronzes. The return of the world championships to Beijing in 2027 therefore presents both an opportunity for, and a clear test of, the current generation of the nation's track and field athletes. Shi Shengji's 200th Asian Games gold was more than a landmark in the record books. It offered a glimpse of what the new generation can offer, and sets a bar for the bigger stages to come. liyingxue@chinadaily.com.cn

item.title: Heritage, modern chic reignite capital's charm
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
Heritage, modern chic reignite capital's charm Commercial vitality boosts Beijing's tourism market appeal Beijing is rapidly revitalizing its consumer market and global tourism appeal through a multifaceted upgrade — seamlessly blending its rich culinary heritage and global gastronomy with cutting-edge retail innovations and enhanced services for inbound travelers. The city recently launched a massive promotional season for its iconic Beijing roast duck along the bustling Wangfujing Street. More than 600 restaurants from over 30 renowned catering brands have joined forces to transform this traditional dish into a dynamic cultural property. Time-honored establishments like Quanjude and Bianyifang are showcasing their national intangible cultural heritage roasting techniques to a new generation of diners. Bianyifang, boasting a history of over 600 years, is introducing creative crossovers such as roast duck pizzas with handmade crusts. Meanwhile, modern culinary innovators such as Da Dong are pushing the boundaries of flavor with their signature "super lean" crispy roast duck. Leading brands are also introducing globalized variations that feature oriental mustard, Thai sweet and sour chili, and Mediterranean aromas. This initiative responds to a growing digital consumption trend, with local data showing a steady increase in online searches and sales for the beloved dish. Recent industry reports indicate that over 1,600 roast duck outlets in Beijing are engaging in online operations, marking a significant year-on-year growth. While dine-in experiences remain the primary consumption scenario, lightweight options like single-serving or half-portion roast ducks have become highly popular in the food delivery sector. To further engage younger demographics and tourists, the campaign introduced a special passport program. Visitors are encouraged to collect stamps across various participating restaurants to win exclusive rewards, effectively turning dining into an interactive city exploration. The promotional materials also feature curated cultural tourism routes, guiding consumers to explore the city's central axis and fashionable districts after enjoying their meals.

item.title: Coercion not the right approach to settling differences
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
Coercion not the right approach to settling differences The European Union's trade policy toward China is acquiring an increasingly familiar look: raise the stakes, set a deadline and hope that Beijing is the one to blink first. Brussels now wants Beijing to accept quotas on selected Chinese exports, including so-called "voluntary export restraints" on electric vehicles, while threatening tougher measures if the October talks fail to produce "tangible" results. EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic is due in Beijing on Oct 8-9, after three months of intensive consultations. There seems nothing irrational about some in Europe worrying about industrial competitiveness or the "trade imbalance". But the mistake is assuming that unilateral pressure is a substitute for consultations. It is not. Trade deficits are economic facts, not diplomatic insults; nor can they be wished away by drawing administrative lines around imports. The proposed "voluntary" export restraints are particularly awkward. Under Article 11 of the World Trade Organization Agreement on Safeguards, members are prohibited from seeking, taking or maintaining voluntary export restraints and similar arrangements. The WTO itself describes such arrangements as "gray-area" measures that the multilateral trading system was designed to eliminate. A quota dressed up as a "voluntary" gesture remains a restriction on trade. Worse, linking Beijing's acceptance of such restraints to Brussels withholding other restrictive measures risks turning negotiations into arm-twisting by another name. That is a poor foundation for the "rules-based" trading order that Brussels says it wants to defend. The European Commission is also considering a new instrument under which tariffs could be triggered when Chinese supplies of certain strategic goods cross a specified threshold. Reports suggest sectors such as semiconductors, chemicals, pharmaceuticals, automobiles and critical raw materials could be affected. Other proposals would make it easier for the EU to activate measures through reverse qualified-majority voting. Such instruments are still proposals, not settled EU law, but their simultaneous emergence is significant: Brussels is constructing a larger toolbox while telling Beijing that October is the deadline. This may look like strength. It also looks like a negotiating party that thinks its arguments are weak. Europe's economic predicament deserves attention, but China should not be asked to accept responsibility for it. The European Commission says the bloc lost 250,000 industrial jobs last year, particularly in energy-intensive industries and automotive supply chains. Its goods deficit with China has exceeded 1 billion euros ($1.13 billion) a day, according to EU officials. But China did not invent Europe's energy costs, productivity problems, regulatory burdens or industrial-policy dilemmas. Nor can tariffs manufacture European competitiveness. There is a simpler question Brussels should ask: why does the EU want to sell more to China while restricting some of the high-tech products China wants to buy? Also European companies would plainly benefit from greater access to the Chinese market. Yet Europe has also tightened scrutiny of Chinese investment and restricted access in strategically sensitive areas. The resulting asymmetry is hardly an advertisement for reciprocity. Chinese manufacturers have not reached global markets through a single magic ingredient called "subsidies". Scale, fierce domestic competition, technological upgrading and investment all matter. Treating every successful Chinese export as proof of subsidy is an easy way to avoid examining the true reasons for the EU's lack of competitiveness. Washington and Beijing have now gone through eight rounds of negotiations without imposing a hard deadline as the basic framework of the talks. Europe's economic relationship with China is hardly less complicated. It therefore seems odd for Brussels to imitate the theatrical elements of US negotiating style while ignoring the prosaic truth that complicated bargains require time. The October meeting should consequently be treated as another stage, not a final exam. China has said that any solution should balance interests, comply with WTO rules and the respective domestic laws of both sides, and take account of businesses on both sides. That is not an unreasonable negotiating position. The EU needs the Chinese market and stable supply chain cooperation; China needs European goods, services and investment, and is open to technology cooperation on the basis of mutual respect. The relationship is not a zero-sum contest between two major economies. If Brussels keeps adding threats to the table, it risks discovering that pressure is much easier to increase than trust. The real test of European negotiating strength is not how intimidating it is when approaching the negotiation table. It is whether it creates enough room at the table for a deal. The economic and trade issues between China and the EU are long-standing. Can the EU realistically expect to resolve them within a few months of establishing a consultation mechanism? In trade negotiations, it is the party that upholds principled positions and remains steadfast amid changing circumstances that demonstrates greater confidence, self-assurance and strength.

item.title: Nation's travel landscape enters new era
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
Nation's travel landscape enters new era Relaxed entry policies, digital payments infrastructure prove a magnet for global tourists As a hand-rowing boat drifts across Hangzhou's famed West Lake, Austrian traveler Florian Eisinger finds himself surrounded by willow-lined shores, ancient temples and centuries of history, with the gleaming skyline of one of China's most dynamic cities rising in the distance. For the 23-year-old who was visiting China for the first time in May, the scene captured what surprised him most about the country. "It was probably one of the most mesmerizing countries I visited in my life," Eisinger said. "From the cities to the landscapes to the people, everything was beyond what I had imagined." Two places stood out. "West Lake is just incredible scenery and a lot of history packed into one 'district', all while you have the very modern city of Hangzhou in the background," he said. "I did a boat tour over parts of the lake, and it was jaw-droppingly beautiful." The other place is Shanghai. Some streets, while being nestled within the bustling heart of the metropolis, especially in the evening, are incredibly beautiful, and it is surreal to imagine this being in one of the largest cities in the world, he said.

What keeps China's high-speed trains so steady? Share - WeChat
A cup of tea can stand upright on a Chinese high-speed train. But the real story isn't the cup. It's the wheel beneath the train. At 350 km/h, the wheel diameter tolerance is tighter than a human hair. Every wheel has its own digital ID. This National Day holiday, millions are traveling home. These wheels carry us safely to our loved ones.

item.title: Leaders pay homage to fallen heroes on Martyrs' Day
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-01
Leaders pay homage to fallen heroes on Martyrs' Day President Xi Jinping and other Party and State leaders attended a ceremony on Wednesday at Tian'anmen Square in central Beijing to present flower baskets to honor fallen national heroes, marking China's 13th Martyrs' Day. Established in 2014 and observed annually on Sept 30, one day before National Day, the day honors those who gave their lives for the liberation of the Chinese people and the nation's development. Since the first observance of Martyrs' Day, Xi, who is also general secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and chairman of the Central Military Commission, has maintained the tradition of paying homage to fallen heroes on this day. On Wednesday morning, Xi and other leaders — Li Qiang, Zhao Leji, Wang Huning, Cai Qi, Ding Xuexiang, Li Xi and Han Zheng — joined representatives from all walks of life for the solemn ceremony in front of the Monument to the People's Heroes. At 10 am, all attendees sang the national anthem, followed by a moment of silence in tribute to the fallen heroes. Nine large flower baskets were placed in front of the monument. Xi and other leaders walked up to the foot of the monument, where he straightened the ribbons on the baskets. Then, they walked around the monument to pay tribute. Among the attendees carrying flowers were veterans, relatives of martyrs, recipients of awards and honorary titles, members of ethnic minority groups, students and children. Liu Jia, an associate professor at Beihang University's School of Marxism, watched the live broadcast of the ceremony. He said that observing Martyrs' Day is not only a solemn tribute to fallen heroes, but also a reminder of the hardships and unwavering convictions forged during China's revolutionary struggles. Liu noted that the commemoration came at a key moment, citing that this year marks the 105th anniversary of the founding of the CPC, the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March — an epic military trek from 1934 to 1936 that helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution — and the launch of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30) for economic and social development. He said that the strength we gain from the Party's glorious history and the Long March will help drive new sci-tech progress today and inspire the younger generation. jihaisheng@chinadaily.com.cn
